Chapter 3: Display Characters

This chapter turns a fixed read view into a user-selected read path. The same service-owned now exposes a managed collection that the component can present through a dropdown-driven selection flow.

The important shift is architectural, not mechanical: selection stays local to the component, while Feature State remains owned by the service. The result is a more interactive read experience without moving State ownership out of the existing boundary.

Add interaction without moving ownership.

A fixed detail view proves that managed State can reach the UI. A useful application lets people decide which record to inspect. This chapter adds that choice without turning a short-lived UI decision into shared Feature State or duplicating the collection in the component.

Why this boundary matters

The character collection remains the service-owned, committed source of truth. A selected id only describes what this component is showing right now. Keeping those responsibilities separate prevents temporary navigation choices from coupling other consumers to this one view.

Use this structure for

  • a master-detail page for customers, products, or records
  • a picker whose choice affects only the current view
  • an interactive read path that will later support editing

By the end of this chapter

You will have a dropdown backed by the committed character collection, a component-local selection Signal, and a reactive detail panel that follows the selected record while the service continues to own the .

Chapter 3 Starting Point and Decision

Start with the completed Chapter 2 project. This chapter changes only example.component.ts, example.component.html, and the component spec. Registration, bootstrap, seed data, and the service remain unchanged.

Confirm the Starting Checkpoint
  1. Run the Chapter 1 project and confirm the first character renders.
  2. Keep ExampleService unchanged throughout this chapter.
Step 1: Add a Dropdown
↑ top

This step upgrades the initial read path from showing the first committed record automatically to letting the user choose which committed record to inspect. The Feature registration, service-owned , and managed collection stay the same; only the UI-facing selection logic changes.

Assume the Angular mechanics are already familiar. Here, keep Feature State in the service, keep selection state in the component, and derive the displayed record from the latest service-owned collection.

Replace the single displayed-character computed Signal with a read-only character collection, a selectedCharacterId Signal, a computed lookup for the selected record, and a small selection handler.

In the template, add a select element that lists the registered characters and keep the detail panel bound to computed controller state instead of reaching into directly.

The matching verification belongs in this same step: the updated component spec should prove the controller starts empty, accepts a valid selection, ignores unknown ids, a Charactersnd renders the selected record without moving ownership out of the service.

Reactive Lookup

The selected character depends on two values: the latest committed collection from the service and the component-local selected ID. When either changes, the computed lookup runs again. A known ID produces its record; an empty or unknown ID produces no selected record and the template renders the empty state.

Make the Change
  1. In example.component.ts, replace the single-record computed value with characters, a computed read of this.#exampleService.state.value() ?? []. 
    {{`readonly characters = computed<readonly StarWarsCharacter[]>(
    () => this.#exampleService.state.value() ?? []
);`}}
  2. Add selectedCharacterId as a local Signal initialized to null. 
    {{`protected readonly selectedCharacterId = signal<number | null>(null);
`}}
  3. Add selectedCharacter as a computed lookup that returns the matching collection record or null. 
    {{`protected readonly selectedCharacter = computed(() => {
  const selectedId = this.selectedCharacterId();
  return this.characters().find(({ id }) => id === selectedId) ?? null;
});`}}
  4. Add selectCharacter(value: string). Convert the dropdown value with Number(value), set the Signal only when that ID exists in characters(), and otherwise leave the current local selection unchanged. 
    {{`protected selectCharacter(value: string): void {
  const character =
    this.characters().find((character) => character.id === Number(value)) ??
    null;

  if (!character) {
    return;
  }

  this.selectedCharacterId.set(character.id);
}`}}
  5. In example.component.html, render one option per characters() entry and pass the selected value to selectCharacter(). 
    {{`<div class="workspace-row workspace-row-top">
  <div class="field selection">
    <label for="character-selection">
      Character ({{ characters().length }} total)
    </label>
    <select
      #characterSelection
      id="character-selection"
      [disabled]="characters().length === 0"
      (change)="selectCharacter(characterSelection.value)">
      <option
        value=""
        disabled
        [selected]="selectedCharacterId() === null">
        Select a character
      </option>
      @for (character of characters(); track character.id) {
        <option
          [value]="character.id"
          [selected]="character.id === selectedCharacterId()">
          {{
            character.fullName ??
              character.name + ' ' + character.lastName
          }}
        </option>
      }
    </select>
  </div>
</div>`}}
  6. Render the details panel only when selectedCharacter() returns a record; otherwise render the empty guidance. 
    {{`<div class="workspace-row workspace-row-bottom">
  <section
    class="panel character-details"
    aria-labelledby="details-title">
    <div class="header">
      <h3 id="details-title">Character details</h3>
    </div>

    @if (selectedCharacter(); as character) {
      <dl>
        <div>
          <dt>Full name</dt>
          <dd>
            {{ character.fullName }}
          </dd>
        </div>
        <div>
          <dt>First name</dt>
          <dd>{{ character.name }}</dd>
        </div>
        <div>
          <dt>Last name</dt>
          <dd>{{ character.lastName }}</dd>
        </div>
        <div>
          <dt>Identifier</dt>
          <dd>{{ character.id }}</dd>
        </div>
        <div>
          <dt>Faction</dt>
          <dd>{{ character.faction }}</dd>
        </div>
        <div>
          <dt class="force-sensitive">Force-sensitive</dt>
          <dd>{{ character.forceSensitiveDisplay }}</dd>
        </div>
      </dl>
    } @else {
      <div class="empty-state">
        <h4>No character selected</h4>
        <p>Choose a character from the list.</p>
      </div>
    }
  </section>
</div>`}}
What to Look For
  • The service still owns the and does not change for this UI enhancement.
  • The selection Signal is presentation state owned by the component, not Feature State owned by the service.
  • The template continues to render computed, display-ready values instead of reading APIs directly.
  • The spec verifies the new UI behavior without changing the -owned Feature State contract.
Step 2: Chapter Round-up
↑ top

The Display Characters chapter is complete once the page starts with no selected character, lists the registered collection in the picker, and updates the detail panel when the selection changes.

The boundary has not moved: the service still owns the and the component still owns only UI selection state.

This is the smallest useful expansion of the initial tutorial: the application moves from one fixed read path to one user-directed read path without changing registration, service ownership, or application bootstrap structure. What changed is the proof that the same service-owned State can now support both an initial empty state and a selected-record view.

Run and Verify
  1. Return to the running Angular application.
  2. Confirm the details panel shows the empty state before a character is selected.
  3. Open the dropdown, choose a character, and confirm the details panel updates to the selected record.
  4. Choose a different character to verify the same read path reacts to the new selection.
  5. In the component spec, submit an unknown ID and confirm the selection remains empty rather than manufacturing or mutating Feature State.
Chapter 3 Summary
  • You should now be able to explain why the collection is shared Feature State
  • Why the selected ID is local presentation state, and how the computed detail reacts to both.
  • Chapter 3 keeps that boundary and adds service-owned create and update requests.
